title: Viktor Frankl
keyWorks: …Saying Yes to Life in Spite of Everything: A Psychologist Experiences the Concentration Camp (1946; in English as Man's Search for Meaning, 1959)
summary: Viktor Frankl was an Austrian psychiatrist and philosopher, the founder of logotherapy, “therapy through meaning.” Having survived the Nazi concentration camps, he concluded that the main driving force in a human being is the “will to meaning,” and that meaning can be found in any circumstances: in work, in love and experience, and in the attitude we take toward unavoidable suffering.
onEmotions: Frankl did not treat feelings as enemies to be eliminated, and he did not see suffering as an illness. He distinguished in a person the body, the psyche and the “spiritual,” or “noetic,” dimension — the capacity to take a stand toward one's own states. From this come his two main tools: “self-distancing” (the ability to look at your fears from the outside, even with humor — this is the basis of “paradoxical intention”) and “self-transcendence” (turning toward work and people beyond yourself — hence “dereflection,” drawing attention away from endless self-observation). He linked many heavy feelings to the “existential vacuum” — the experience of meaninglessness — and answered them with “tragic optimism”: the capacity to say yes to life in spite of suffering, guilt and finitude.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is not a weakness or a malfunction — it's a sign that you care about what happens next. Frankl, a physician and psychotherapist, paid special attention to “anticipatory anxiety”: we start to fear the anxiety itself, we wait for it — and the waiting is exactly what brings it on. It becomes a closed loop. To break it, Frankl proposed “paradoxical intention” — not fighting the anxiety but telling it, with a touch of humor: “Go on then, show me what you've got.” This works thanks to a distinctly human capacity he called “self-distancing”: the ability to step back from yourself a little and look at your state from the outside, even with a smile. You are not the same as your anxiety — you are the one who notices it. It's easier to accept once you no longer have to defeat it.
anxiety.practice: Say to your anxiety silently, exaggerating a little and with a smile: “Come on, worry harder, I'm watching.” Notice what changes when you stop fighting it.

fear.text: Fear is a natural response to something that could hurt you; there's no need to be ashamed of it. Still, Frankl insisted on one distinction: a person and their feelings are not the same thing. We have a psyche with its fears and impulses, but we also have what he called the “spiritual,” or “noetic,” dimension — the capacity to take a stand toward our own states. He liked the thought that a person doesn't have to put up with everything that goes on inside them. Fear can be right there, speaking loudly — and still not decide for you. Frankl called this “the defiant power of the spirit”: not the absence of fear, but the freedom to act in keeping with what matters to you while the fear is still here. You can be afraid and remain yourself.
fear.practice: Name your fear in one sentence, then add: “And still, what matters to me is…” — let it be one value, not a plan of action.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and it doesn't need to be fixed right away. Frankl pushed back against the idea that people seek above all pleasure and calm. He called the human being “homo patiens” — a creature able to suffer without losing meaning. From his point of view, sadness often carries the sound of what is dear to you: we grieve over what has value for us. Of the three paths to meaning he wrote about — work, experience and the attitude toward the unavoidable — the third matters especially here. Even when circumstances can't be changed, you keep the freedom of how you carry your sadness: gently, honestly, without turning away. Sadness lived this way is not empty time but part of your life, and it means something too.
sadness.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm sad because what's dear to me is…” — and leave it without judgment.

grief.text: Grief is the price of love, and it needs no justification. Frankl himself lost many of those closest to him during the war, and he wrote about grief with great care. One of his central ideas is the past as a “granary”: what has been lived does not vanish but is kept in the past forever, and nothing can undo it. He told of an elderly doctor who was struggling badly after his wife's death. Frankl asked him: what if he had died first? “For her this would have been terrible,” the man answered. Then his pain appeared in a different light: he had taken on himself the suffering he had spared her. The grief doesn't disappear because of this, but it gains a meaning — and becomes something that can be carried.
grief.practice: Recall one moment with the person you lost that is now forever “stored in the granary.” Describe it to yourself in three or four details.

quote.text: In some way, suffering ceases to be suffering at the moment it finds a meaning, such as the meaning of a sacrifice.
quote.author: Viktor Frankl

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and there is nothing shameful in it. Frankl believed that human beings are by nature directed beyond themselves — toward another person or toward a task. He called this “self-transcendence”: we become ourselves not when we're focused only on ourselves, but when we are turned toward someone or something. From this angle, loneliness is not a defect but a longing for that turning-toward; it simply lacks someone to be addressed to right now. Frankl noticed that it helps a person to know that somewhere there is someone or something waiting for them — a person, a task, a book they haven't finished writing. Such a bond can exist even at a distance, even when no one is nearby.
loneliness.practice: Write down who or what in the world might be waiting for you — a person, a task, something you've started. Even one line counts.

anger.text: Anger is a strong and honest feeling; it usually flares where something important has been touched. Frankl didn't demand that people get rid of their feelings. For him freedom is not freedom from emotions but the freedom to take a stand toward them. Between what happens to us and what we do, there is room for choice, and in that room lies our responsibility. From this angle, you can ask your anger not “how do I suppress you?” but “what are you standing up for?” Often there is a value behind it: fairness, respect, care. Once you see it, anger stops being just a flare-up and becomes a hint about what you truly hold dear. And how you answer that hint is your decision.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm angry because what matters to me is…” — and name the value that was touched.

shame.text: Shame is heavy: it feels as if what's bad isn't what you did, but you yourself. Frankl firmly objected to this confusion. He spoke of the “unconditional value” of every person: human dignity doesn't depend on success, on mistakes, or on how “useful” someone is. A person, for Frankl, is always more than any one of their actions and any one of their moments. He also emphasized the capacity for “self-distancing”: you can look at what makes you ashamed from the outside — as an episode, not a verdict. From this angle, shame shows that you have a sense of how things ought to be, and that speaks in your favor rather than against you. But it doesn't define who you are.
shame.practice: Describe what you're ashamed of in the third person, in one or two calm sentences, as an episode from someone's life rather than a verdict.

guilt.text: Guilt is unpleasant, but it speaks of a living conscience. Frankl placed guilt in the “tragic triad” of human life, together with suffering and mortality. None of us escapes it. He called his answer to this triad “tragic optimism”: the capacity to say yes to life in spite of everything. In the case of guilt, this means turning it into an opportunity to change for the better. Conscience, for Frankl, is the “organ of meaning”: it senses what a situation asks of us. Guilt shouldn't become endless self-punishment; its meaning lies in a response — to put right what can be put right, and to become a little different where nothing can be undone.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: “What one small action would be a response to this guilt, rather than a punishment for it?” Write it down.

envy.text: Everyone knows envy, and it says a lot about our desires. Frankl insisted that meaning is unique: it is particular to each person and each situation. Life, he said, doesn't pose its questions to humanity in general but to you specifically, in your specific situation — and no one can answer them for you. From this angle, you might say that envy is an attempt to answer someone else's question. Another person's life looks brighter, but its tasks are not yours. Yet envy can also be used as a hint: what you envy often hides a value that matters to you too. Then the question changes: not “why them and not me?” but “what in this do I want — in my circumstances?”
envy.practice: Name what you envy and ask yourself: what value lies behind it, and what might it look like in my life, on a small scale?

emptiness.text: Emptiness — the sense that nothing has any meaning — is very heavy, and you are not alone in it. Frankl described it as the “existential vacuum” and considered it one of the main afflictions of his age: instincts no longer tell people what they must do, and traditions no longer tell them what they should do. Importantly, he did not regard this as an illness or a weakness. Concern about meaning, for Frankl, is a deeply human experience. He proposed a turn he called “Copernican”: it isn't we who ask life about its meaning — it is life that questions us. And we answer not by reasoning but by concrete, small deeds. The emptiness doesn't have to be filled all at once; it's enough to hear one small question of this hour.
emptiness.practice: Ask yourself not “what is the meaning of life?” but “what does this day expect of me right now, in the next hour?” Write down the first honest answer, even a very small one.

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal state when life has posed a question that doesn't yet have an answer. Frankl's comfort here is that meaning, in his view, doesn't need to be invented — it needs to be discovered, and it is always tied to a concrete situation. He spoke of the “meaning of the moment”: you don't have to know the meaning of your whole life to see what today is asking of you. Conscience helps with this — Frankl called it the “organ of meaning,” an intuitive sense of what would be right here and now. It works quietly and doesn't hand out ready-made plans. From this angle, confusion is not a failure but a time of listening. One clear small thing can turn out to be a better answer than trying to sort everything out at once.
confusion.practice: Out of everything that's tangled right now, pick one small question you already know the answer to, and write it down.

fatigue.text: Tiredness is a signal worth listening to, not a reason to scold yourself. Frankl warned against a dangerous confusion: a person's value is often mistaken for their usefulness. But dignity, for Frankl, is unconditional and doesn't depend on how much you've done. He also described three paths to meaning, and activity is only one of them. The second path is experience: music, nature, someone close, simply a quiet presence. The third is the attitude toward what can't be changed. When there's no strength for doing things, the other two paths stay open. From this angle, you might say that rest isn't a fall out of a meaningful life but part of it: experience, too, fills life with meaning.
fatigue.practice: Choose one simple experience for the next five minutes — the view from the window, a song, a warm drink — and let yourself simply take it in, without doing anything.

boredom.text: Boredom is unpleasant, and people are often ashamed of it, though it tells us a lot. Frankl took boredom seriously: he noticed that people of his time suffered less and less from want and more and more from boredom. He described the “Sunday neurosis” — the slump that comes when the weekday rush dies down and the inner emptiness becomes visible. For Frankl, boredom is one of the faces of the “existential vacuum”: a longing for something worth living for. But it's not a verdict — it's a question. Boredom doesn't say “something is wrong with you”; it says “look for what will call you.” For Frankl, meaning doesn't push, it pulls; and boredom can be the first step toward noticing that call.
boredom.practice: Remember the last time time flew by without your noticing. What were you doing, and for whom? Write it down in one line.

joy.text: Joy is a wonderful state, and it's worth simply living it. Frankl offered an interesting view of it: happiness, he said, can't be pursued — it must “ensue” on its own, as a side effect of devoting yourself to a task or to another person. The more we chase happiness, the more surely we miss it. So joy that has come on its own is a sign that you're truly connected to something right now. Frankl also spoke of “experiential values”: taking in beauty, friendship, love in itself makes life meaningful. And what has been experienced, in his view, is kept forever in the past — it can no longer be taken away. There's no need to analyze this joy; you can simply let it be.
joy.practice: Stay in this joy for one more minute and notice: what or whom is it connected to? Tell yourself: “This happened, and it will remain.”

love.text: Love is one of the deepest experiences, and Frankl considered it the second great path to meaning. For him, love isn't just attraction or merely an emotion, but a way of seeing another person in their uniqueness. When we love, we notice not only who a person is but also who they could become — their not-yet-realized possibilities. And by seeing them, we help them come true. Frankl wrote that even when the beloved isn't near, their image can sustain us: love is directed at the very core of a person and doesn't depend entirely on their physical presence. From this angle, love isn't something that “happened” to you, but something that enriches your life, even when it isn't easy.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and write down one of their possibilities that you can see but that they may not yet notice in themselves.

quote.text: Love is the only way to grasp another human being in the innermost core of his personality.
quote.author: Viktor Frankl

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and it's good to cherish it. Frankl gave it an unexpected philosophical foundation. The pessimist, he wrote, sees only the “stubble field of transitoriness” — what passes and disappears. But he overlooks the full granaries of the past, where the harvest has already been brought in: deeds done, love lived, trials borne with dignity. Everything that has been, for Frankl, is preserved forever — he even considered “having been” the most secure kind of being, because nothing can undo it anymore. From this angle, gratitude is the ability to see those granaries. It doesn't deny difficulties; it remembers that good things happened too and belong to your life.
gratitude.practice: Write down three things that are already “stored in the granary” of your past and that no one can take away from you.

hope.text: Hope is the soul's natural movement toward the future. Frankl spoke of “tragic optimism”: an optimism that doesn't deny suffering, guilt and the finitude of life, but persists in spite of them. His first book after the war was titled “…Saying Yes to Life in Spite of Everything.” Hope in this sense isn't the certainty that everything will be fine, but faithfulness to what is dear to you, even without guarantees. Frankl emphasized that it's easier for a person to hold on when there is something ahead worth living for — a task, a meeting, a person. You don't have to know how things will turn out. It's enough to know what you are turned toward, and that already gives you footing.
hope.practice: Finish the sentence: “Even if things don't turn out the way I want, what will still matter to me is…”

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a bittersweet feeling, and there's a lot of love for what has been lived in it. Frankl offered an image that explains it well. Imagine a person who tears sheets off a calendar and watches anxiously as there are fewer and fewer. Another person carefully files away each sheet he tears off, having written on the back what happened that day — and rereads them with joy. For Frankl, the past is not lost but preserved: what has been remains “having been” forever, and that is the most durable kind of being. From this angle, nostalgia is not only longing for what's gone but also a meeting with what is already yours forever. The past doesn't need to be brought back in order to keep nourishing you.
nostalgia.practice: Recall one day from the past that you long for, and write “on the back of the sheet” three of its details you'd like to keep.

craving.text: A craving is a strong feeling, and there is nothing disgraceful in it. Frankl noticed that when the striving for meaning — he called it the “will to meaning” — finds no outlet, its place is often taken by the “will to pleasure”: the wish to drown out the emptiness with quick relief. From this angle, a craving often points not only to its object but also to what's missing right now: rest, closeness, the sense of being needed. Frankl also said that a person doesn't have to put up with everything that goes on inside them: you can feel an urge without identifying with it. A craving is like a wave: it rises, peaks and subsides. You can wait it out by watching it, rather than obeying it.
craving.practice: Rate the strength of the craving from 1 to 10 and ask yourself: “What am I really missing right now?” After a few minutes, rate it again.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure or a sign of weak character. Frankl, who worked as a physician, spoke of the “mass neurotic triad” of his time — depression, aggression and addiction — and linked it in part to the “existential vacuum,” the experience of meaninglessness that belongs to a whole era, not to one person. This means your struggle is not solely your personal fault; it is woven into the way society lives. Frankl stressed something else too: a person always keeps a dimension of freedom — the capacity to take a stand toward themselves, however small. The way out of addiction is rarely walked alone, and seeing in it a search for meaning, not just a fight with a habit, is already a step along it.
addiction.practice: Write down one thing you'd like to be freer for. If you have the strength, think about who you could talk to about it — someone who understands, or, for example, a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A heavy morning after — both in body and in mind — is familiar to many, and there's no need to add self-flagellation to feeling unwell. Frankl said that guilt can become “an opportunity to change for the better,” not a reason for endless punishment. If there's something about yesterday you don't like, it simply means your conscience is alive — Frankl called it the “organ of meaning.” But there's a simpler thought too. For Frankl, every day asks us its own questions, and this one does as well. It doesn't demand heroics. Even when you feel wrecked, you can answer one small question of the day: take care of something small, call someone, do one thing calmly.
hangover.practice: Ask yourself: “What one small thing can I do today to take care of myself or someone else?” — and choose something truly manageable.

euphoria.text: Euphoria is a vivid feeling of uplift, and you can be glad of it. Frankl spoke of “experiential values”: moments when the world opens wide and life feels full make it meaningful in themselves. Yet he noticed something subtle: happiness can't be held on to if you chase it — it comes as a consequence, and trying to grab it tighter scares it off. Frankl called this excessive effort “hyper-intention.” From this angle, it's better not to hold euphoria in a fist but on an open palm: to live it without demanding that it last forever. And what has been experienced, for Frankl, doesn't go anywhere — it will always remain part of your life.
euphoria.practice: Describe to yourself in one sentence how this uplift feels — in your body and in your thoughts — without trying to prolong it.

crash.text: The comedown after a high can be very hard, and it's not your fault. Frankl would offer two supports here. The first is about the past: whatever was good isn't cancelled by the slump. The high has already happened and, in Frankl's view, is kept forever in the “granary” of the past; it wasn't an illusion just because it ended. The second is about freedom: even when we don't choose our state, we keep the freedom of how we relate to it. No heroics are required — it's enough not to take the present heaviness for the final truth about yourself and about life. The slump is part of a movement, not a verdict. And you can treat it gently, like hard weather that will also pass.
crash.practice: Write: “Right now it's hard for me, and still there was…” — and name one good thing from the recent high that is already yours forever.

panic.text: Panic is frightening: your body seems to sound the alarm, your thoughts race. This feeling deserves to be taken seriously. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Frankl worked a great deal with “anticipatory anxiety” — the fear of a repeat, which itself sustains what it fears. He noticed that a desperate struggle with this state often feeds it, while the ability to step back even slightly and look at it from the outside — he called this “self-distancing” — loosens its grip. Your task right now is not to defeat the wave but to wait it out, leaning on what is simple and bodily. You are the one who notices the wave, and it passes through you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and feel the support beneath you. Take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and silently name five things you can see.

dread.text: An oppressive fear of the future is a heavy feeling, and it calls for special gentleness toward yourself. Frankl himself stood more than once before enormous uncertainty and knew how it weighs on you. His answer isn't a promise that everything will be fine, but a reminder of what remains in your hands. We don't choose many of our circumstances, but we do choose how to relate to them — Frankl called this the last freedom, the one that can't be taken away. He also advised looking not at the whole future at once but at the next step: each moment has its own meaning, and it can be discovered even when the far horizon is hidden in fog. You don't have to bear the whole future at once — only today.
dread.practice: Write down one thing you can do today, and one thing you can let go of for now because it isn't in your hands.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out is a very human feeling: it seems that real life is happening somewhere else, and you're not there. Frankl has a thought that turns this fear upside down. Each moment, he wrote, offers many possibilities, but we can actualize only one. By choosing, we decide which of them will become reality and be preserved in the past forever. From this angle, a choice is not a loss but the rescue of one possibility from nonbeing. Besides, meaning, for Frankl, is different for everyone: life poses its questions to you, in your circumstances. Other people's parties and trips answer other people's questions. Your “here” is no worse than someone else's “there” — it's simply yours.
fomo.practice: Name one possibility you're choosing right now, instead of what you're “missing out on.” Tell yourself: “This will become part of my life forever.”

sleepless.text: A sleepless night wears you down, and there's no need to be angry with yourself about it. Frankl noticed a striking pattern: some things slip away the moment you start demanding them. Sleep, like happiness, can't be seized by effort. The harder we try to fall asleep and the more closely we watch whether it's working, the further sleep recedes. Frankl called this “hyper-intention” (excessive striving) and “hyper-reflection” (excessive self-observation). His answer is “dereflection”: gently turning attention away from the task of falling asleep itself. From this angle, you can stop demanding sleep from the night and let it simply be a time of rest. Lying in the quiet is rest too.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself: “I don't need to fall asleep right now; it's enough just to lie here and rest.” Shift your attention to the feel of the blanket and to slow breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what you leaned on collapses. Your pain and anger here are legitimate. Frankl would help you see two things. First: what you put into this relationship — trust, love, care — was real, and someone else's act doesn't cancel it. For Frankl, the past is preserved forever, and your faithfulness in it remains yours. Second: betrayal is the other person's act, not a verdict on your worth. Human dignity, for Frankl, is unconditional. What remains is the freedom he considered inalienable — the freedom of how you relate to what happened. It doesn't require you to forgive right away, and it doesn't require you to forget anything. It only means that the last word about you doesn't belong to the one who let you down.
betrayal.practice: Write: “What I gave in this relationship was real, because…” — and add one piece of evidence.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a tormenting and very human feeling: in it, the fear of losing is mixed with love. Frankl understood love as the ability to see another person in their uniqueness. From this angle, you might say that jealousy lives in comparison — “what if someone is better?” — while love is directed at what is unique: at what can't be compared. By his logic, your own uniqueness can't be “replaced” either. Frankl noted that jealousy risks turning the beloved into property to be guarded — and thereby missing love itself. This isn't a reproach: jealousy is often born of fear. But you can ask it: what am I really afraid of, and what am I asking for?
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentences: “My jealousy is afraid that…” and then “What it's asking for is…” Don't send this to anyone — just look at it.

resentment.text: Resentment is the long trace of injustice, and you don't need to hurry to “let it go.” Frankl, who lived through enormous injustice, knew the past can't be changed. But he insisted: only what happened is unchangeable, while our attitude toward it remains free. He considered this freedom the last one that cannot be taken away. From this angle, resentment is a state in which another person's past act keeps deciding for us how we live. Frankl didn't demand forgiveness on command. He only suggested asking: what does this situation ask of me now? Sometimes the answer is to protect your boundaries, sometimes to speak about the pain, sometimes to get on with your own life.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: “If this resentment became a little smaller, what would I spend the freed-up energy on?” Write down the answer.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart truly hurts, and this pain reflects how much the love meant. Frankl has a thought that may comfort you: the meaning of love doesn't vanish when a relationship ends. Love, for Frankl, is one of the main paths to meaning, because in it we see another person in their uniqueness. And that experience has already taken place: it is preserved forever in the past, in the “granary” where everything lived is stored. No breakup undoes it. This doesn't mean you should cling to what's gone. It means you came out of this love not emptied but enriched, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. The pain will pass, and the value will remain.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing this love opened up for you — about the world, about people or about yourself — that will stay with you.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're an “impostor” about to be found out is familiar even to very experienced people. Frankl would explain it through “hyper-reflection” — excessive self-observation: when all your attention goes to the question “am I good enough?”, the work itself fades into the background, and you only get more anxious. His answer is “dereflection”: shifting attention from yourself to the task and to the people it's done for. Frankl also wrote that success shouldn't be aimed at directly: like happiness, it comes as a consequence of dedication to a cause. From this angle, the question “do I deserve this?” can be replaced with another: “what does this task, and these people, need?”
impostor.practice: Reframe the anxious thought “will I manage?” into the question “what does this work need right now?” — and write down one concrete answer.

self_hatred.text: When you hate yourself, the inner voice sounds merciless and seems like the only truth. It isn't, and you don't have to agree with it. Frankl taught that every person's value is unconditional: it doesn't depend on mistakes, on successes, or on what you think of yourself right now. He also said that a person doesn't have to put up with everything that goes on inside them — and this applies to a cruel inner critic too. You can notice this voice without accepting its verdict. Frankl called this “self-distancing”: you are not only what speaks in you, but also the one who hears it. And there is more in you than that voice is willing to admit.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one cruel phrase from your inner critic, and next to it, how a kind friend who knows you well would answer it.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is one of the heaviest experiences, and it's not your fault. Frankl knew it from his own life: he went through the Nazi concentration camps, where almost nothing depended on the individual. It was there that he formulated the idea that even in such conditions a person keeps a last freedom — the freedom of attitude. It's important to understand this correctly. It isn't a reproach (“you're choosing your attitude badly”) but a consolation: some inner footing remains to you, even if everything outside is out of your hands. Frankl stressed that what can be changed is worth changing; and where nothing can be changed, we can still choose how to carry what is happening.
helplessness.practice: Divide a page into two parts: “doesn't depend on me” and “depends on me, even a little.” Write at least one small thing in the second column.

quote.text: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way.
quote.author: Viktor Frankl

procrastination.text: Putting things off is neither laziness nor a vice; behind it there's often fear, tiredness or a lack of clarity. Frankl would perhaps see “hyper-intention” here too — an excessive striving to do things flawlessly, which paralyzes. The higher the stakes, the harder it is to begin. His answer is to return to the “meaning of the moment”: life doesn't ask about the whole project at once, but about what can be done now. Frankl considered responsibility the very essence of human existence, but he understood it not as a burden but as a response: a situation poses a question, and you answer it with a deed. The answer can be very small. Sometimes it's enough to open the file, write one sentence, make one call.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: “What's the smallest answer I can give this task in the next two minutes?” — and name it.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a real loss, and there's no need to play it down. Frankl knew what it's like to lose your former world: after the war he returned to Vienna, where much and many were gone, and built his life anew. His philosophy suggests that meaning isn't tied to a place. The three paths he wrote about — work, experience and the attitude toward what can't be changed — are open everywhere. And the past, for Frankl, isn't left behind: everything you have lived is preserved forever and belongs to you, wherever you move. From this angle, you can carry your roots with you, and in a new place gradually look for what will call to you.
uprooted.practice: Write down one thing from the past that you've “taken with you,” and one that could become a small task or joy of yours in the new place.

overload.text: Overload from the endless stream of news, tasks and messages is a real burden, not a weakness of yours. Frankl said that in an age when traditions no longer tell people what to do, each person has to discern for themselves what matters in every situation. He even put it this way: if the Ten Commandments no longer hold for many, a person needs to learn to hear the “ten thousand commandments” hidden in ten thousand situations. For that, according to Frankl, you need a sensitive conscience — the “organ of meaning” that helps you pick out what matters most. From this angle, the way out of overload isn't to get everything done but to ask: which of this is really addressed to me?
overload.practice: Of everything pressing on you right now, pick one thing that is really addressed to you. Set the rest aside for five minutes.

unreality.text: The feeling of unreality — when the world or you yourself seem far away, as if behind glass — is frightening, and it's important to describe it gently. Frankl didn't write about this state directly, but his thought can offer some footing. For him, meaning is always concrete: it lives in this minute, this encounter, this task, not somewhere in general. Among the paths to meaning he named “experience” — simply taking in what's nearby: a sound, a color, a person. From this angle, you might say that what brings us back to reality isn't reasoning about it but the world's small, concrete responses. You don't need to feel everything at once; one clear thing you can touch is enough.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object near you and silently name three of its qualities: weight, temperature, texture. Linger on each one.

awe.text: Awe is the feeling of the world opening up, vast and beautiful. You don't need to explain it to enjoy it. Frankl gave such moments great importance: he called them “experiential values” and believed that a single such moment can make a whole life meaningful. He recalled how even in the harshest conditions of the camp, people could stand still before a sunset and say: how beautiful the world could be. Beauty, for Frankl, isn't a luxury but one of the forms of meaning. And what you're experiencing now will forever remain part of your past — in his view, the most secure kind of being. Let yourself simply be in it.
awe.practice: Stay in this feeling for a minute without doing anything. Then write down one word you'd like to give it.

relief.text: Relief is a wonderful feeling: something heavy has let go. It's worth noticing and living it. Frankl believed a certain tension is natural to human beings — between what is and what could be; it's a normal part of a life turned toward meaning. But relief is the moment when what held you in tension has finally been resolved. From this angle, you might say it's time to gather the harvest: what you have endured is already preserved forever in the past, in the “granary” where everything lived is stored. Don't rush straight on to the next task. Let yourself notice that you made it through — that's part of the meaning too.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and tell yourself: “That's behind me, and I got through it.” Notice where in your body things have become lighter.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and it's worth enjoying. Interestingly, Frankl didn't consider total calm the highest human goal: he argued against the idea that we strive only for equilibrium without any tension. What a person needs, in his view, is not a care-free emptiness but something worth living for. But this is no reproach to calm. From this angle, you might say that real calm isn't emptiness but a silence in which you can hear better. In such moments it's easier to hear the “meaning of the moment” — the quiet question life is asking. Or you needn't look for anything at all: the experience of calm itself, for Frankl, is one of the “experiential values.”
calm.practice: Stay in the calm for a minute. If something wants to make itself heard — a thought, a wish, an image — simply note it, without deciding anything.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful surge when you want to create. Frankl considered this one of the three paths to meaning: “creative values” — what we bring into the world through deeds, creativity, work. He stressed that meaning doesn't push a person from within, like an instinct, but pulls from outside: you are called by what hasn't been done yet, and that you in particular can do. Inspiration, from this angle, is the sensation of that call. Frankl also spoke of self-transcendence: we become most ourselves by giving ourselves to something larger than ourselves. There's no need to analyze inspiration or to fear losing it. Best of all is simply to start answering the call.
inspiration.practice: Write down one concrete action with which you can answer this inspiration today, and start it, even if only for five minutes.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is an awkward feeling: rejoicing at someone else's failure seems shameful. But everyone has it, and it says little about what kind of person you are. Frankl taught that between feeling and action there is a space of freedom: what matters isn't what flared up in us but what stand we take toward it. He valued in people the capacity for “self-distancing” — the ability to look at yourself from the outside, even with humor. From this angle, you might say that schadenfreude is often tied to comparison: someone else's failure briefly shrinks your own sense of not being enough. Once you notice this, the feeling loses its power. And the unconditional value Frankl spoke of belongs both to you and to the one who stumbled.
schadenfreude.practice: Notice the schadenfreude and tell yourself gently, with a smile: “Aha, comparing again.” Ask: what do I want for myself in this story?

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling: as if another person were beneath you. It often appears when someone has badly offended your values, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. Frankl, however, consistently refused to judge people by categories. He wrote that there are only two “races” of people — the decent and the indecent — and they are found in every group, among all kinds of people. From this angle, contempt risks replacing a concrete person with a label, while Frankl believed that everyone has unconditional dignity and the possibility of change. This doesn't mean approving of what others do. You can clearly reject an act and still not reduce the person to it.
contempt.practice: Split your note into two parts: “What exactly in this act is unacceptable to me” and “Which of my values it offended.”

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, almost physical feeling, and it can be directed at people, at situations and even at yourself. It's natural: it's the voice of the boundary of what you consider acceptable. Frankl would perhaps see in it a reflection of values — we are repelled by what contradicts what matters to us. When disgust is turned on yourself, Frankl has two thoughts. First, a person doesn't have to put up with everything that goes on inside them — you can disagree with your disgust at yourself. Second, human dignity is unconditional and isn't cancelled by actions, by the body or by any state. The feeling may be strong, but it doesn't pass a final verdict.
disgust.practice: Name what exactly disgusts you, and add: “This offends my value of…” If the disgust is at yourself, ask what someone who respects you would say to you.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and you want justice restored. The wish itself isn't a crime but a sign of a wounded sense of justice. Frankl knew its force well. He described how some people, freed after enormous injustice, thought they now had the right to act unjustly themselves. And he answered, gently and firmly: the evil you have suffered gives no right to do evil to others. Frankl didn't demand that anger be suppressed or that you forgive right away. He suggested asking: what is this feeling protecting? Usually it's dignity, boundaries, the truth. These can be defended without causing harm, and that too expresses the freedom he valued.
revenge.practice: Finish the sentence: “What I want most is for it to be acknowledged that…” This will show what your wish is really protecting.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can be very strong, and then comes shame. But being angry with the people you love is human: closeness makes us vulnerable. Frankl said that love sees in another person not only who they are now but who they could be. Anger often flares in the gap between the two. From this angle, it doesn't contradict love but can be its other side. Frankl also stressed the freedom of taking a stand: a feeling comes on its own, but what we do with it is our choice. If you lost your temper, guilt can become not a punishment but, as he put it, “an opportunity to change for the better” — for example, to come back and talk.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has eased a little, finish the sentence: “I'm angry because what matters to me is…” — and think about how to say this to your loved one without reproach.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is a very common state in close relationships, and it doesn't make your love any less real. Frankl distinguished several dimensions in a person: the bodily, the psychological — character, habits, moods — and the spiritual, that is, the unique core of the personality. Love, in his view, is directed at bottom toward that core. From this angle, you might say that irritation often concerns habits and traits, while love concerns the person themselves. Both feelings can be true at once. You don't have to choose one and cancel the other. You can hold both and ask: what in this person is dear to me, what is hard for me — and what of this can we talk about?
ambivalence.practice: Divide your note into two columns: “What is dear to me in them” and “What I find hard to bear.” Look at both without crossing either out.

guilty_relief.text: Relief that you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a gravely ill loved one — is very common and very understandable. Relief doesn't cancel love. Often it means that a long suffering has ended: yours, theirs, or both. Frankl helps you see this differently. In his view, everything you gave that person — care, strength, time, love — is preserved forever in the past, in the “granary” from which nothing is lost. Relief doesn't erase it. Frankl also wrote that suffering can have a meaning, such as the meaning of a sacrifice — which means it also has a natural end. You can grieve and, at the same time, feel that it has become easier to breathe.
guilty_relief.practice: Write two sentences: “I feel relief because…” and “I loved and cared, and that was…” Let both be true.

indifference.text: Indifference where something “should” move you is frightening: it seems something is wrong with you. But it's often a defense. Frankl, recalling his camp experience with great restraint, described how people in unbearable circumstances fell into emotional numbness — it protected the soul when feeling everything was no longer possible. He insisted, in general, that an “abnormal” reaction to an abnormal situation is normal. Indifference can also be a manifestation of the “existential vacuum” — a general weariness from meaninglessness. From this angle, it doesn't make you an unfeeling person. It's a sign that your strength is at its limit, and your feelings will most likely return when it's safer.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself without reproach: “What might this numbness be protecting me from right now?” Write down the first thing that comes to mind.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything and run away — from a job, a city, a role — is familiar to many, and it doesn't make you irresponsible. Frankl would perhaps hear a signal in it: what you're doing no longer resonates with meaning. He wrote about the “existential vacuum” — the feeling that life runs on inertia rather than on a calling. From this angle, the wish to escape can be a distorted form of the “will to meaning”: you don't want to go “nowhere,” but to a place where there will again be something to live for. Frankl gave no recipes for big decisions. He suggested listening to conscience — the “organ of meaning” — and asking yourself: what do I want to go toward, not only what do I want to get away from?
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I could run away, I'd want to be somewhere where…” See which value shows up in your answer.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” — unavailable, or the “wrong” person — can be embarrassing and unsettling. But the feeling itself speaks of a living heart, not of some corruption in you. Frankl distinguished several levels at which one person attracts another: the bodily, the psychological — being charmed by someone's character or manner — and the deepest, directed at the unique person. From this angle, you can ask: what exactly draws you so strongly to this person? Behind attraction there is often a value or possibility you'd like in your own life: freedom, lightness, recognition, depth of conversation. You don't need to judge yourself or decide anything right away; you can first understand what this feeling is about.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down three qualities that draw you to this person, and ask yourself: which of these is missing from my own life?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and of their judgment is agonizing, and very many people have it. Frankl described a mechanism that is easy to recognize here: “hyper-reflection” — excessive self-observation. When, in a conversation, you keep watching how you sound, how you look, whether you're blushing, your attention closes in on yourself, and the awkwardness grows. Frankl's answer is “dereflection”: shifting your attention from yourself to the other person or to the topic of conversation. He also used “paradoxical intention” with a touch of humor: instead of fearing that you'll blush, mentally “wish” to blush as brightly as possible. What's funny loosens fear's grip. You don't have to be flawless; it's enough to be turned toward the other person with interest.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, give yourself one task: notice something interesting about the other person — one detail, thought or word.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: when it's unclear what will happen, it's hard to make plans and hard to calm down. Frankl knew this feeling in its extreme form — life with no known end date, when no one knows how or when it will all be over. He noticed that people bear the unknown more easily when they have a “why”: a person they want to see, a task they want to finish. The future may stay foggy, but meaning, for Frankl, belongs to every moment, and it can be discovered right now. From this angle, uncertainty isn't a void but an open space in which you can still choose what to lean on.
uncertainty.practice: Write down your “why” — one person, task or value for whose sake it's worth getting through this uncertainty.

quote.text: He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Twilight of the Idols; quoted by Frankl in Man's Search for Meaning

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — is exhausting: time seems to have stopped. Frankl described the danger of a “provisional existence” — a state in which life is postponed “for later,” and the present feels like nothing but a waiting room. He noticed that a person who stops seeing meaning in the present day finds uncertainty especially hard to bear. But for Frankl every moment has its own meaning, and it doesn't begin only after the answer arrives. This day is your life too, not a pause before it. From this angle, you can wait and live at the same time: do something small, spend time with someone, notice something beautiful. The waiting won't disappear, but it will get lighter.
waiting.practice: Ask yourself: “While I wait, what can this day give me, or ask of me?” Choose one small task or experience.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do is painful, but it shows that how you live matters to you. Frankl had a particular way of relating to the past. On the one hand, what has happened can no longer be changed. On the other, everything good that was is also preserved forever and can't be taken away. And regret, in his view, can become a lesson for the future. He even formulated a kind of rule of logotherapy that helps you feel the weight of every choice. This isn't a call to torment yourself but an invitation: since the past has made you wiser, let that experience serve what you choose today.
regret.practice: Finish the sentence: “If this happened now, I would…” — and think about where in your life there's a similar situation in which this knowledge will come in handy.

quote.text: Live as if you were living already for the second time and as if you had acted the first time as wrongly as you are about to act now!
quote.author: Viktor Frankl

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is an aching, very personal feeling. It shows how much that person means to you. Frankl has a deeply lived observation about this. In the hardest days of his life, in the camp, he talked with his wife in his mind, not knowing whether she was alive. And he understood that love is directed at the very core of a person and doesn't depend entirely on their being physically near. The image of a loved one can sustain, console, give strength. From this angle, longing is not only the pain of distance but also a sign of a living bond. The person you long for is still present in your life — in memory, in your conversations with them, in who you became beside them.
longing.practice: Write this person a few lines — not to send, but simply to talk with them.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from heavy news, wars, injustice — is neither an exaggeration nor a weakness. It shows that you care. Frankl would call it an expression of “self-transcendence”: human beings are by nature turned beyond themselves, toward others. He also wrote that an abnormal reaction to an abnormal situation is normal behavior. How do you carry this pain? Frankl didn't call for turning away. He proposed “tragic optimism” — not denying suffering, but looking for what you can do within your own circle: support, help, act with decency. He was convinced that decent people are found everywhere — and what you do in small ways matters.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small kind act that's within your reach today, in your own circle. And allow yourself to set the news aside for a while.

quote.text: An abnormal reaction to an abnormal situation is normal behavior.
quote.author: Viktor Frankl

rejection.text: Rejection wounds: it feels as if it wasn't an offer or a relationship that was turned down, but you as a whole. This pain is real. Frankl helps separate the one from the other. He insisted on the “unconditional value” of every person: your dignity doesn't depend on whether you were accepted or not. A refusal speaks of the meeting of two people, two situations, but it doesn't pass a verdict on you. Moreover, meaning, for Frankl, isn't exhausted by one person or one opportunity: life keeps asking you questions, and there will be new ones among them. From this angle, rejection isn't the end of the road but a turn, where you can ask: what is truly addressed to me now?
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: “I wasn't chosen, and still I remain a person who…” — and name one real quality of yours.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is a deep and very early fear; there's nothing shameful in it. It speaks of how important the people close to you are. Frankl would offer two supports here. The first is unconditional dignity: your worth doesn't vanish if someone leaves. The second is self-transcendence: a person finds meaning by turning not toward one single person but toward the world — toward people, tasks, experiences. From this angle, you might say that the fear of abandonment narrows the world, as if your whole life hung by a single thread. When there are more threads — friendship, work, activities you love — the fear doesn't disappear, but it stops ruling everything.
abandonment.practice: Draw or write down the “threads” that connect you to the world: people, tasks, places, joys. Mark at least three.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts badly, and this pain deserves gentleness. Frankl saw in love a way to grasp another person in their uniqueness, and believed that this very seeing makes the one who loves richer. From this angle, you might say that even unrequited love isn't meaningless: it revealed something precious in another person to you, and in that discovery you grew. Love, for Frankl, is one of the “experiential values,” and everything experienced remains in the past forever. At the same time, reciprocity doesn't arise on demand, and its absence doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Your capacity to love like this is part of you, and it isn't going anywhere.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love revealed to you — in the other person and in yourself. What do you now know about your capacity to love?

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it's as if you've been stripped of your dignity. Frankl knew this firsthand — his experience in the concentration camps was also an experience of systematic humiliation. It was there that he gained the conviction that there is an inner dignity that cannot be taken away. Others may treat us unjustly, but they cannot cancel our unconditional worth. And this is no reproach to those for whom it was too hard to “hold on”: Frankl wrote about people with enormous compassion. From this angle, humiliation speaks of the other person's act, not of you. You can feel a burning pain and at the same time remember that your dignity is still yours.
humiliation.practice: Say to yourself, aloud or silently: “I was treated in an unworthy way. That says something about the act, not about me.” Write down one thing you respect yourself for.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be very painful, and a huge number of people know it. Frankl would describe it through “hyper-reflection” — constant self-observation, when your attention returns again and again to how you look. Such observation, in his view, only intensifies the suffering. Frankl's answer is “dereflection”: turning your attention toward the world, toward a task, toward people, toward what you feel and experience, rather than how you look from the outside. He also insisted that a person can't be reduced to a body: there is a unique personality in them, which is what love sees. Your body isn't a rating; it's the way you are present in the world.
body_shame.practice: Recall one thing your body let you experience today — a taste, a touch, a walk, a hug. Thank it for that.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, is a hard trial, and you have every right to tiredness, fear and anger. Frankl, as a physician, thought a great deal about how people live through illness. He stressed: what can be changed is worth changing — taking care of yourself and seeking help. But there is also what can't be changed, and here, for Frankl, the third path to meaning opens — “attitudinal values”: the way a person bears the unavoidable. He called the human being “homo patiens” — able to suffer without losing meaning. And most importantly: your worth doesn't depend on how healthy or “useful” you are. Illness changes your possibilities, but it doesn't cancel you.
illness.practice: Write down what is even slightly within your power to change right now, and what you are simply carrying for now. Notice how you carry the second — with what quality.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy and well-earned feeling; you can be glad of it. Frankl called activity and creativity the first path to meaning — “creative values.” What you've done has brought something into the world that wouldn't have been there without you. And for Frankl, what has been done is preserved forever in the past: it's like a calendar sheet on the back of which you wrote what happened that day — and you can reread it with pride and joy. No one will take from you what has already been accomplished. Frankl only warned against chasing success for its own sake; but the joy of work done for the sake of the work itself is exactly meaning showing itself in life.
pride.practice: Write down what exactly you did and what was hardest about it. Let yourself reread it with pleasure.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a subtle feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness. It doesn't need fixing. Frankl thought a lot about transitoriness: everything passes, and that can make us sad. But his answer was unexpected. What is transitory, in his view, are only possibilities; once they are actualized, they are rescued and preserved forever in the past. So transitoriness doesn't make life meaningless — on the contrary, it gives weight to every moment and to our responsibility for it. From this angle, melancholy is a sense of fragility and of preciousness at the same time. In it, you feel that every moment is unrepeatable. Let this feeling stay with you for a while.
melancholy.practice: Notice one fleeting thing around you — a light, a sound, a scent — and tell yourself: “This happened, and now it is forever.”
